newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Vranitzky says Albania snap election will be safe.
newsitem.headline: Vranitzky says Albania snap election will be safe.

text.p: European envoy Franz Vranitzky told the Albanian people on Thursday the international community would do its best to ensure a fair and safe election on Sunday despite a resurgence of violence in the anarchic south.

Speaking live on Albanian state television's main evening news bulletin, the envoy of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) overseeing the snap vote said it would be a turning point in the troubled nation's history.
"The election on Sunday will be one of the most important political decisions that the Albanian people have to take," Vranitzky said in English.
"We will take care that the election can be held and dangers that might be in the hearts or minds of the people will be minimised as best as we can," he added.

Vranitzky, a former Austrian chancellor, said he was confident polling stations would close earlier than originally planned to help ensure the safety of voters and hundreds of international observers.
"This will add to the safety and security of the whole election process," he said.

The opening hours of the 4,525 polling stations across the country had been one of the last stumbling blocks in the preparation of the election, called in March to put an end to months of unrest sparked by the collapse of dubious investment funds earlier this year.
The final decision on whether stations can close by 6 p.m. rather than by 9 p.m. is now in the hands of the Albanian constitutional court.
But Vranitzky told a news conference earlier on Thursday that the central electoral commission would decide to do so anyway.

Nearly 500 international observers, including 112 parliamentarians from 22 countries, are set to fan out around the mountainous Balkan country on Friday to prepare for the first round of the election on Sunday.

Campaigning by the parties has been at best sporadic, with both President Sali Berisha's Democrats and their main rivals, the Socialists, unable to hold rallies in areas dominated by rival supporters and outside police or government control.

Even some soldiers in the 7,000-strong multinational protection force deployed in Albania in April following widespread violence have been told by their national capitals to stay away from certain towns and the remote countryside.

In the southern port town of Vlore, where a rebellion erupted in March in response to the collapse of several local pyramid funds, daily exchanges of gunfire between local warlords escalated on Thursday into more widespread violence.

Finance Minister Arben Malaj, a Socialist, narrowly escaped from a gunbattle and was forced to take shelter in a seaside hotel after an election rally in a sports hall was broken up by volleys of gunfire and the building later set on fire.

The protection force said Italian army commanders had despatched two platoons and two armoured personnel carriers to evacuate civilians from the smouldering building. Local police said one person was killed and at least two injured during the day's violence.
Calm returned to Vlore later, but a candidate for an ethnic Greek party said her father was being held near the town of Gjirokaster by men demanding her withdrawal from the vote.
Like most of southern Albania, Gjirokaster and Vlore are run by so-called "Salvation Committees" violently opposed to Berisha and hoping the election will force him from office.
Vranitzky acknowledged that conditions for holding an election in the impoverished country were not ideal, but said postponing the vote would have made matters even worse.
"It's clear to everyone that these times are not easy for Albanians. But there are many countries in the world who wish to be good friends with the Albanians," he said.
